summary: Discusses the signals that on-path network elements can observe from transport protocols, contrasting implicit signals with explicit ones. For example, the clear-text messages of TCP's state machine are often used by network devices, while encrypted transports expose less. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When cars on a road show their turn signals, others know what is coming. This document talks about what signals network protocols give to devices along the way, and how it differs when messages are hidden.

questions: implicit vs explicit signals in transport protocols
how does encryption affect firewalls and nat
subtitle: What network devices learn from the visible parts of transport protocols, and what the IAB recommends when those parts are encrypted.

tldr.problem: On-path network elements such as firewalls and NATs have long inferred information from clear-text transport messages like TCP's handshake. Encrypting transports removes those signals.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB lists the signals that can be inferred, compares four options for what to do, and recommends encryption by default, with explicit signals only when the sender intends the path to use them.
tldr.outcome: Implicit signals should be avoided, and an explicit, integrity-protected signal should replace one only when its originator wants network elements to use it.

today: RFC 8558 is an Informational IAB document from April 2019 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the IAB's recommendation and notes that discussion of mechanisms was continuing when it was written.

sections.title: Implicit Signals on the Path
sections.content:
RFC 8558, from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB), looks at the signals that on-path elements get by examining transport protocols. TCP's state machine uses well-known messages exchanged in the clear. They exist to create state between the two endpoints, but network elements along the path commonly treat them as signals for their own functions. This is an implicit signal.

A firewall may create a pinhole rule when it sees the initial TCP SYN acknowledgement for a connection started from inside, and remove it on seeing a RST or a FIN and ACK exchange. When a transport encrypts the fields it uses for state mechanics, these signals are no longer available, and path elements fall back on their configured defaults.
sections.eli5: A doorman watches people knock and wave to learn who is allowed in. If everybody wears a cloak and stays silent, the doorman must guess.

sections.title: Signals That Can Be Inferred
sections.content:
Signals come either from direct examination of packet sequences, such as a sequence number gap pattern that suggests unreliability, or from association, such as timing a flow's packet inter-arrival times. The RFC groups them as follows.

  • Session identity: a tuple of visible header information used to track a flow.
  • Routability and intent: the two hosts can reach each other and want to keep talking. This justifies the firewall pinhole and, in some devices, assumptions such as Endpoint-Independent Mapping or Filtering (RFC 7857).
  • Flow stability: load balancers may keep a flow on one path to avoid reordering.
  • Resource requirements: table space in a firewall or NAT, or reservation of radio air time, energy or capacity.
  • Path latency and reliability: measured from exposed timestamps or sequence numbers, and from retransmissions and gaps.

The list is illustrative, not exhaustive.
sections.eli5: Helpers along the road can tell a lot just by watching: who is traveling together, how fast, and whether some packets got lost.

sections.title: Four Options
sections.content:
The RFC offers four alternatives that optimize different things and calls its conclusion preliminary.

  • Do not restore the signals. Elements apply their own defaults. Experience is not extensive, but state tables for such flows are generally not kept as long, so heartbeat traffic must keep NAT or firewall bindings alive. A QUIC connection-id may help load balancers keep a flow's path.
  • Network-layer signals. IPv4 has few facilities, but IPv6 hop-by-hop headers (RFC 7045) might suit; deployability needs more examination.
  • Per-transport signals. There is a risk the first transport to develop them gets reused for other purposes, simply because it traverses NATs and firewalls better.
  • Signals common to several transports. Transports layered on UDP might share one mechanism, which has a better chance of avoiding ossification.
sections.eli5: You can do nothing, put the signal on the envelope, give each kind of mail its own signal, or invent one shared signal for many kinds of mail. Each choice has a downside.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
The IAB urges protocol designers to design for confidential operation by default, encourages encryption by default in implementations, and urges firewall policy administrators to permit encrypted traffic. It accepts that implicit signals will be lost as a result. Implicit signals should be avoided, and replaced by an explicit signal only when the originator intends network elements to use it.

Any method should follow these principles:

  • Signaling meant for end-system state machines should be protected by confidentiality and integrity protection so only the end systems see it.
  • Anything exposed to the path should be intended for use by path elements, and should be integrity protected so endpoints can detect changes.
  • Path-facing signals should be decoupled from the signals that drive endpoint state machines, to avoid creating opportunities for more inference.
  • Intermediate elements should not add visible signals that identify the user, origin node or origin network.

The RFC adds that on-path actors cannot verify integrity protection unless they share keys with the end systems or a common set of trust points, so integrity can generally be verified reliably only by endpoints. Managing authentication of on-path signals is outside its scope.
sections.eli5: Keep private things in a sealed envelope by default. If you want helpers to see something, write it on a separate label made just for them, and do not let it reveal who you are.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Path-visible signals let elements act on them. If an attacker controls the element, it can drop, delay or mishandle packets, and may characterize or fingerprint the communicating nodes from the pattern of signals. Adding visible signals gives observers more information and may reduce user privacy when it can be linked to a node or user.

Signals independent of the endpoints' state mechanics may be falsified without affecting the peer's view of the flow, and for encrypted flows on-path devices cannot detect this. Designers should consider how falsified signals would affect operation, and operators should avoid defaults that encourage gaming the system with false signals.
sections.eli5: Any label you stick on the outside can be read by a snoop or faked by a cheat, so each label must be added carefully.
